title: Follow an edge — contour direction and turns
materials: A shoe, shell, or simple tool with a readable outside edge
A second small object for a brief transfer, if drawing from life

concepts.name: Notice where an edge changes direction

objective: Draw a shoe, shell, or tool while following several changes in its visible edge direction; compare and correct two turns on the same drawing, then transfer one turn to a second object.

haveReady.subject: A shoe, shell, or simple tool with several readable changes in its outside edge, plus a second object for one short transfer if drawing from life.
haveReady.setup: Place the first object so its full useful edge is visible from one steady side view. Keep HB and an eraser nearby. Choose a second object only for the short transfer at the end; it does not need a full drawing.
haveReady.referenceRoute: Draw from life when convenient. Otherwise use the supplied fixed side-view shoe reference. For the transfer, use a second object at hand or reuse the fixed spoon reference from Lesson 04; keep each view steady while drawing.

explanation: A contour follows the visible boundary where an object meets its surroundings. Look along a short stretch of that edge; its direction changes at turns. Record those changes from the object instead of drawing a remembered symbol.

A visible edge can stop behind another part or become hard to see where the tones meet. For this study, follow the outer edge you can actually see. Two small corrections on the same drawing are enough; the line does not need to be dark or perfectly smooth.

exercise.instructions:
1. Keep the shoe, shell, or tool in one steady view. With HB, draw a light, recognizable outline, looking back at the object as you go.
2. Choose one short stretch of the outline that changes direction several times. Follow that same edge slowly, noticing where it bends and which way it turns.
3. Compare two turns in that stretch with the visible edge. Revise those two short bends on this same drawing; keep the rest of the outline as it is.
4. Choose one clear turn on a second object and draw a short contour through it. If using supplied references, the Lesson 04 spoon view is a ready second object. Compare the turn with its object or fixed view, make one small adjustment if useful, then stop.
exercise.source: A shoe, shell, or simple tool from life, or the supplied fixed side-view shoe reference; transfer one turn to a second object at hand or the fixed Lesson 04 spoon reference.

reflection: Where did the edge change direction, and what did you notice when you followed one turn on a second object?

teaching.whyItMatters: Following a visible edge through its turns helps a contour describe the particular object in front of you. Comparing two turns gives you evidence for a small correction before you try the same attention on another object.
teaching.connections: Lessons 01–04 established light, adjustable marks, pencil contact, and same-drawing correction. This lesson follows an edge through several direction changes; Lesson 06 shifts attention to the whole outside shape before its parts.

compare: Follow the same short edge on the shoe, shell, or tool in your drawing and in the object or fixed reference. At two turns, compare where the edge bends and which way it changes direction. On the second object, compare your single turn with that object's visible boundary; keep each comparison in its own fixed view.
correct: On the first drawing, change only the short segment around the two turns that differ from the observed edge. Keep the other contour as it is; if an old line distracts, use the scrap-tested eraser method from Lesson 04 or leave the faint guide. On the second object, adjust only the short contour around its one selected turn, then stop.
selfCheck: Can you point to several places where the subject's outside edge changes direction?
Did you revise two turns on the original drawing while leaving the rest of its outline alone?
Could you follow one turn on a second object without drawing it all over again?
deepDive: A contour is a choice about which visible edge to follow. It may end where one part passes behind another, and it may become difficult to see when the neighboring areas have similar tone. Do not extend an unseen edge just to complete an outline; record the parts the subject actually shows you.

A turn is useful because it marks a change in the path, not because it needs a special line style. Look for where the edge begins to bend and where it changes direction again. On the second object, following only one turn lets you test whether that looking habit transfers without repeating the whole study.
